https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
This is the Troy School District Business Services Update delivered at the Board Retreat on March 8, 2025 and filed as agenda item 5.H for the March 18, 2025 meeting. It combines the 2025-26 budget calendar, an explainer on school funding mechanics, the 2024-25 Amendment 2 adjustments, and fund-by-fund detail on the ancillary funds.

The budget schedule runs: April–May, develop 2025-26 budgets and 2024-25 final amendments; June, public hearing and millage rate adoption; June, adoption and 2024-25 budget amendment (final, all funds); June–October, audit of 24-25 financial statements and federal programs.

The funding explainer is the document's substantive core. It presents the foundation allowance as the sum of three components and traces them across five years. State sources ran $6,251, $6,523, $6,733, $6,971 and $6,804 from 2020-21 through 2024-25. Local non-homestead levy ran $2,030, $2,121, $2,355, $2,637 and $2,804. Hold harmless, levied on homestead property, ran $1,034 then $786 in each subsequent year. The totals are $9,315, $9,430, $9,874, $10,394 and $10,394 — flat between 2023-24 and 2024-25, with the composition shifting further toward local sources as the state share fell $167 per pupil. For 2024-25 the presentation notes $3,590 of the total is dependent upon voter approval. Other revenue sources are listed as sales, income, use, liquor, excise, cigarette and lottery taxes.

The headline finding follows: for 2024-25, the foundation allowance of $10,394 is $4,236 per pupil less than the inflation-adjusted foundation allowance, and that per-pupil deficit equates to approximately $51.9 million in lower revenue for Troy School District this school year. This is the district's framing of its structural funding position and the number that underpins subsequent budget-reduction discussions.

Amendment 2 revenue adjustments represent a 1.4% increase from Amendment 1. State source revenue reflects an audited FTE count of 12,272 and a foundation of $10,394, with 31aa Mental Health at $1.1 million and a 147g 3% reimbursement at $1.6 million. Federal revenue includes Title carryover of $250,000, Water First of $55,000 and Effective Technology of $20,000. Further state source items are a prior year adjustment of $600,000 and section 32n Out of School Time of $240,000. Transfers include a GASB 87 entry of $525,000.

Amendment 2 expenditure adjustments represent a 1.9% decrease. Salaries and benefits are adjusted for current staffing and lane adjustments as well as new Schedule C items; grants are updated to reflect all carryover and final allocations; and debt service and capital outlay reflect GASB 87 leases of $525,000.

The ancillary funds section first defines each fund: Food Service for the district's food service program; Community Service for fee-for-service programs including the CARE company and community recreation; Troy Preschool for the preschool program; TCC Grant Fund for the Troy Career Center (Michigan Works! Troy); and Sinking Fund for the sinking fund millage.

The Food Service Fund highlights note the contractual obligation reconciled, a projected $1.2 million use of fund balance, a projected $2.4 million fund balance, $1.6 million remaining excess fund balance, and $1.4 million set to be spent on the Troy High kitchen. The accompanying table shows 2023-24 actual revenues of $6,789,099 against a recommended 2024-25 budget of $7,545,293 — State $4,847,963, Federal $2,343,186, Local $354,144 — with expenditures rising from $6,204,143 actual to $8,731,566 recommended, driven by Supplies and Materials at $4,188,216, Purchased Services at $2,919,708, Capital Outlay at $825,000 and Repairs and Rentals at $655,000. Net change in fund balance moves from a positive $584,956 to a negative $1,186,273, with the ending balance falling from $3,600,167 to $2,413,894.

The Community Service Fund reports revenues and expenditures reconciled to year-end expectations, a projected $(278k) operating deficit, a projected $1.8 million fund balance, and a reminder that there are no federal childcare stabilization funds in FY2025. Its table shows 2023-24 actual revenue of $1,963,870 against a recommended $1,827,940, with expenditures rising from $2,190,378 to $2,106,093 recommended — Salaries $761,694, Employee Benefits $379,851, Purchased Services $894,048, Supplies $55,500, Capital Outlay $15,000. Net change moves from $(226,508) to $(278,153) and the ending fund balance from $2,099,551 to $1,821,398.

The Preschool Fund reports a $95,000 projected operating surplus and $2.3 million projected fund balance, flagging the Governor's Universal Preschool initiative for 25-26 and the same absence of federal childcare stabilization funds. The TCC Fund reports revenues equal to expenditures. The Sinking Fund reports a $433,000 projected operating surplus and $509,000 projected fund balance.

This is Barton Malow Builders' bid evaluation and award recommendation for Bid Package #5, the Administration Building Renovation, dated 8/26/2025. It is addressed to Dan Trudel, Assistant Superintendent of Business Services, from Evan Chechack, Project Manager, and filed as agenda item 4.a at the September 2, 2025 meeting. Bid proposals were received and read publicly on August 12, 2025, and Barton Malow reviewed them with the project architect and engineer, TMP Architecture Inc.

The recommendation covers eight trade categories. Selective Demolition (02 4119) goes to Reese Contracting, Inc. at $45,500. General Trades (06 0000) goes to LMS Construction at $173,117. Due to recent performance concerns on similar Barton Malow bond programs, we are not recommending to the lowest General Trades and Carpentry bidder." Mechanical drew eleven bids from $598,000 (Contrast Mechanical) to $787,172 (Goyette Mechanical), with Watson Bros. only $2,000 higher at $600,000. Electrical drew nine bids from $154,000 (E.L. Electrical) to $297,335 (Allied Building Service Company of Detroit).

This is the First Amendment to the Amended and Restated Pupil Transportation and Transportation Fleet Maintenance Services Contract, entered into as of July 1, 2025 and attached to the underlying contract dated July 1, 2022, between Troy School District — a Michigan general powers school district at 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, Michigan 48098 — and First Student, Inc., a Delaware corporation at 191 Rosa Parks Street, Suite 800, Cincinnati, Ohio 45202. It appears as agenda item 3.b. at the June 3, 2025 meeting.

The recital states the parties desire to exercise a Renewal Term and also amend the Contract Rates and other terms.

Clause 1 addresses the renewal term. Pursuant to Section 2.2 the district exercises its option to extend, but the parties agree to modify Section 2.2 and extend for two years commencing July 1, 2025 and expiring June 30, 2027. Thereafter the district has the option to extend by up to one additional year on a year-to-year basis, subject to written approval in its sole and absolute discretion, with rates for any extension term mutually agreed under Section 10.3. The clause states explicitly that nothing requires the district to exercise the extension option and that the contractor has no expectation of a contract beyond the renewal term.

Clause 2 replaces Exhibit B of the contract in its entirety with the amendment's own Exhibit B. Clause 3 amends the notice provisions: notices to the district go to the Superintendent at 4400 Livernois Road with a copy to Jeremy S. Motz, Esq. of Clark Hill PLC, 220 Park Street, Suite 200, Birmingham, Michigan 48009; notices to the contractor go to First Student's Area General Manager at 120 Hart Avenue, Troy, Michigan 48098 with a copy to FirstGroup American's General Counsel in Cincinnati.

Clause 4 is a change-in-law provision terminating the district's obligations if federal or state law makes payment of the rates illegal, impracticable or impossible. Clause 5 requires written agreement for further modification, clause 6 ratifies the contract as modified with the amendment controlling in the event of conflict, and clause 7 permits execution in counterparts.

Exhibit B sets out the pricing assumptions. Daily route charges are billed per route per day, where a route comprises AM tier runs, any mid-day or shuttle runs, and PM tier runs operated by the same bus in the same package; a mid-day or shuttle run not incorporated into an AM/PM package is charged separately. Charges assume an average daily route time of 6.0 hours calculated gate to gate from the district's transportation facility. Field trips, athletic trips and extra-curricular trips are invoiced hourly in quarter-hour increments.

The pricing is predicated on the district operating 175 days per academic year for general education routing, with one free dry run per route before school year start. A 175-day "Academic School Year Minimum" applies to regularly scheduled routes to cover fixed costs, and the district is not charged for routes on days school is not in session provided services are cancelled per Section 10.1, with three exceptions. On snow days the district is charged 80% of the daily route charge for each route not operated, provided the contractor demonstrates all drivers were paid at their normal rate — if the contractor fails to pay or document such payment, the charge drops to 40%. For intermittent closures caused by power outages or similar events, where the district operates fewer than 180 days requiring transportation, the charge is 40% of the daily route charge for each route not operated below 175 days. For extended closures beyond ten consecutive school days, the district pays 70% of the current cost per route per day if the contractor keeps a qualified trained driver in active employment receiving at least daily minimum pay, keeps all other staff — the site manager, dispatcher, router and one mechanic — in active status at full pay, pays all wages at prevailing rather than discounted rates, and performs all other services; or 25% if the driver is not in active paid status. The district may elect the 25% option at its discretion. As a condition of payment, within five days of each payroll cycle the contractor must make available all books and records on wages paid, with charges adjusted and overpayments reimbursed if the conditions are not met.

Further terms provide that the district supplies the fuel, with the contractor liable for costs of any misuse; that a material change in route volume — defined as 10% or more in either direction — triggers good-faith renegotiation; and that extension-term adjustments follow Section 10.3.

The rate schedule covers 2025-2026 and 2026-2027, with all charges inclusive of bus maintenance services. General education daily route charge, based on 6.0 hours daily route time and covering 33 routes, rises from $306.78 to $334.39. The in-district special needs route charge for 17 routes rises from $454.93 to $495.87, as does the out-of-district charge covering 7 routes, which includes Wing Lake routes. Mid-day runs and shuttles, 24 of them, charged hourly per run where not attached to a route, rise from $78.33 to $85.38. The special needs summer route charge covering 20 routes rises from $379.63 to $413.80. Extra-curricular and athletic trips, charged hourly with a one-hour minimum, rise from $69.91 to $76.20. Transportation aides rise from $33.63 to $36.66 per hour. White fleet maintenance is charged hourly for labor with parts at cost, at rates to be mutually agreed before work is performed. Across the board the second-year increase is approximately 9%.

What it is
The OCSBA redline of its 2025 recommended amendments to previously adopted resolutions, circulated to member districts with a stated rationale beneath each change. Resolutions approved by at least nineteen member districts become the Association's official position.

Substantive amendments
- **Accountability and Transparency** — expanded to name FOIA requests and the Open Meetings Act explicitly, and to cover community-governed districts, charter schools, cyber schools, community colleges and public universities. Rationale: expanded to include FOIA, OMA and additional school entities.
- **Broadband** — "we support" replaced with "OCSBA supports" throughout, and a new bullet added supporting dedicated cybersecurity resources. Rationale: cybersecurity is a growing issue needing dedicated funding.
- **Mental Health** — "provide adequate state resources" replaced with "providing, at a minimum, annual inflation adjusted state resources." Rationale: districts need consistent, annual funding.
- **School Aid** — items A and D were duplicative; the constitutional Pre-K-12 restriction and voucher opposition moves to the first bullet, and the June 1 budget enactment deadline becomes item D.
- **SFRC** — reference to "recommended additional studies on capital costs, infrastructure, and transportation" removed. Rationale: those studies have been completed, so OCSBA now supports all SFRC recommendations.
- **School Nutrition** — "expansion of the Free and Reduced Meals program to include all children as was done during the pandemic" replaced with "codification of free universal meals."
- **Early Childhood** — renamed from "Universal Preschool." Rationale: public preschool dollars should not be used for vouchers or private and parochial preschools; mandatory kindergarten added because kindergarten is not currently mandatory in Michigan.
- **Aligned associations** — COSSBA added, since MASB belongs to both NSBA and COSSBA.

This is the Oakland County School Boards Association's "Bylaws – Amendments at a Glance" document, circulated alongside the full bylaws redline for member district consideration in May 2025. It separates the proposed changes into those that are purely clerical and those revised for content, giving the affected page, article and section plus a rationale for each.

Four revisions are identified as clerical or grammatical in nature and stated not to change the meaning of the bylaws. In Article V Section 3, Place of Meeting, the truncated word 'oƯ' is corrected to 'office' — the rationale notes it is supposed to read 'office'. In Article VIII Section 2, Term of Office, the stray word 'Ther' is corrected to 'The' by deleting the trailing r. In Article IX Section 4, concerning the Government Relations Committee, the rationale describes adding 'on' after 'information' for grammar and clarification. In Article XIV Section 2, Dealing with the Association, a duplicated phrase is removed — the original text repeats "or between the Association and one or more of its directors or officers".

Eight further sections are revised for content.

Article VII Section 4, Notice, currently permits notice of special Board meetings delivered personally, by phone, fax or email, or by five days' notice by mail, with mailed notice deemed delivered on deposit in the US mail in a sealed envelope with postage prepaid. The revision deletes the language referring to US mail and fax, with the rationale that these are outdated modes of communication.

Article VII Section 10 is added in full: the Board of Directors shall create and maintain Board Operating Procedures to be used in conjunction with the bylaws. The rationale notes the Board recently adopted Board Operating Procedures that further define roles, responsibilities and timelines.

Article VIII Section 6, the Secretary, retains the existing duties — attending all Board meetings, recording votes and minutes in a book kept for that purpose, giving notice of meetings, and executing conveyances and contracts with the President — and adds that at the discretion of the Board of Directors on an annual basis, the Office of Secretary may be divided into two roles, Corresponding Secretary and Recording Secretary. The rationale is that with a Board of seven to nine directors, splitting the role is helpful and provides additional leadership opportunities.

Article IX Section 3, Committee Chairs, moves the timing of the annual chair election from the first order of business at the committee's first meeting after January 31st to after July 1st. The rationale is that the operating year runs July 1 to June 30, so the change brings committee elections into alignment. The seven calendar days' written notice requirement is unchanged.

Article IX Section 4, the Government Relations Committee, retains the standing committee designation, the purpose of receiving legislative information for sharing with member districts, and the minimum of six meetings per year. Membership and leadership provisions are set out, including that a chairperson is elected annually from appointed members at the first committee meeting after January 31st, each member district in attendance having one vote cast by its appointed representative, and that in the absence of an elected Vice Chair the Vice President of OCSBA assumes the position. The rationale is to ensure leadership is being built on the GRC.

Article IX Section 5, the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee, changes who appoints committee members from the Board of Directors to the OCSBA President annually, with members eligible for reappointment and the appointed members electing a chairperson at their first meeting after appointment. The Government Relations Committee Chairperson is to be a member of the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee. The rationale is that common practice is for the OCSBA President to make committee appointments.

Article XV Section 5, Method of Giving Notices, replaces "mailing" with "electronic communication" and directs notice to a director or officer's last known district-provided email address, with notice deemed given at the time of such communication rather than such mailing. The rationale is that OCSBA does not physically mail communications.

Article XVI Section 1, Amendments, retains the requirement that bylaws be altered or amended by vote of the member school districts on written ballot with at least a forty-day voting period and one vote per district, and adds that grammatical errors which do not change the meaning or intent of the language may be corrected by the Board of Directors without a vote of the membership. The rationale is that small grammatical and spelling errors that do not change meaning or intent can be corrected by the Board during the annual review rather than requiring a membership ballot.

The first opposes partisan school board elections in response to House Bill 4588. What it is
The OCSBA resolutions circulation dated 2026-01-09, presented to member districts with two proposed new resolutions plus the full set of continuing resolutions. Adoption requires approval by at least nineteen member districts.

Proposed resolution #1 — non-partisan school board elections
"OCSBA supports non-partisan school board elections." Framed as a response to House Bill 4588, then moving through the Michigan House. The rationale argues partisan elections would decrease the number of willing candidates; increase campaign costs, since members would have to win both a primary and the November election; align local education decisions with party interests rather than student needs; and exclude thousands of current or potential board members, including federal employees who are legally prohibited from running in partisan races.

Proposed resolution #2 — Early On Michigan
"OCSBA supports full funding of Early On Michigan, an early intervention program for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with disabilities, developmental delays or are at risk for delay(s) due to certain health conditions."

The rationale sets out the statutory framework: Michigan's Mandatory Special Education law requires services from birth through age 25; IDEA Part B covers ages 3 through 21 and Part C covers birth through age 2, which Michigan calls Early On. Local communities receive funding through their ISD, each with an interagency coordinating council.

The funding gap is quantified:
- Estimated annual cost of high-quality early intervention — **$230 million**
- What the state should appropriate (60%) — **$138 million**
- What Section 54d of the FY26 School Aid Act provides — **$48 million**

The rationale notes the congressional promise to fund 40% of special education costs applies to Part C as well as Part B.

This is the Oakland County School Boards Association resolutions document dated 2026-01-09, circulated to member districts and appearing in the Troy board packet for December 9, 2025. It presents two proposed new resolutions with extended rationales, followed by the full set of continuing resolutions. The governing threshold is stated at the top: under OCSBA Bylaws Article IX Section 5, resolutions approved by at least nineteen member school districts become the official position of the association.

Proposed new resolution #1 reads: "OCSBA supports non-partisan school board elections." The rationale identifies the trigger as House Bill 4588, then moving through the Michigan state House, and links to the bill. Four arguments are advanced against partisan school board elections. They would decrease the number of willing candidates. They would increase campaign costs, since school board members would have to be successful in two elections — a primary as well as the November general. They would align local education decisions with party interests rather than student needs. And they would exclude thousands of current or potential board members, including federal employees, who are legally prohibited from running in partisan races.

Proposed new resolution #2 reads: "OCSBA supports full funding of Early On Michigan, an early intervention program for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with disabilities, developmental delays or are at risk for delay(s) due to certain health conditions."

Its rationale is the more developed of the two. It opens by stating the need to shine a light on the importance of early intervention programs such as Early On, and the need for additional state funding both to adequately serve families of children already identified as eligible and to serve all children who should be identified.

The statutory framework is set out carefully. The Michigan Mandatory Special Education law, or MMSE, requires special education services for eligible children and students from birth through age 25. Federal law also mandates early intervention. Part B of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act covers special education services for students ages 3 through 21. Part C of IDEA covers early intervention services for eligible infants and toddlers from birth through age 2, and in Michigan Part C is called Early On. Special education supports for students aged 22 through 25 fall under MMSE. The rationale notes OCSBA has always supported early childhood education, and that the earlier intervention begins, the greater the impact.

Early On is described as Michigan's statewide, comprehensive, coordinated interagency system of early intervention services for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with disabilities and their families, coordinated by the Michigan Department of Education under IDEA Part C. Local communities receive funding through their local Intermediate School District, and each ISD jurisdiction has an interagency coordinating council comprising individuals from human service agencies, parents, educators and other agency personnel who serve families. Implementation is also guided by local memoranda of understanding between education, mental health, public health and social services.

The funding case is quantified. For fifty years the Association has advocated for IDEA funding, and the congressional promise to fund 40 percent of the cost of providing special education services applies to Part C — early intervention for infants and toddlers through age 2 — as well as to Part B for children aged 3 to 21. While federal advocacy continues, the rationale states state funding is woefully lacking for Early On: the estimated annual cost of providing high-quality early intervention services is $230 million; the state should appropriate at least $138 million, or 60 percent of that estimated cost; and Section 54d of the FY26 School Aid Act provides state funding of just $48 million. A link is given to the Early On Foundation's case-for-funding document.

The closing clause lists the NSBA, MASB, OCSA and COSSBA legislative agendas as aligned.

Agenda item 2.g. — the bond authorizing resolution for the 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), prepared under the School Bond Qualification, Approval and Loan Act. The November 8, 2022 General School Election approved bonds in one or more series not to exceed **$555,000,000**. - Refunding of the 2016 School Building and Site Bonds dated December 28, 2016, maturities May 1, 2027 through May 1, 2032
- Combined single series: **not to exceed $220,000,000**, with a separate capital projects fund maintained for the Projects

Senior managing underwriter Huntington Securities, Inc.; bond counsel Miller, Canfield, Paddock and Stone, P.L.C. — with its periodic representation of Huntington in unrelated matters expressly disclosed and approved; municipal advisor PFM Financial Advisors LLC.

This is the resolution authorizing the Troy School District's 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), County of Oakland, State of Michigan, drafted by bond counsel and filed as agenda item 2.g. The resolution's own text records it as offered and adopted at a regular meeting of the Board held in the School District on November 18, 2025 at 7:00 p.m. local time, certified by Emina Alic, Secretary of the Board of Education; the packet itself is filed against the November 11, 2025 meeting.

The recitals establish the authorization chain. At the General School Election held November 8, 2022, the qualified electors approved the issuance of bonds, in one or more series, in an amount not to exceed $555,000,000 — the 2022 Bond Proposal — for remodeling, equipping, re-equipping, furnishing and re-furnishing school buildings, athletic fields, playgrounds and other facilities; erecting and completing, equipping and furnishing a replacement middle school and classroom additions and other additions to existing school buildings and facilities; acquiring and installing instructional technology infrastructure and equipment; and acquiring, preparing, developing and improving sites and the purchase of school buses. Under Article IX Sections 6 and 16 of the Michigan Constitution of 1963, tax levies for those bonds are without limitation as to rate or amount.

The first series was the 2023 School Building and Site Bonds dated March 7, 2023, in the original principal amount of $171,370,000. A separate recital notes that due to prevailing market conditions at the time of sale, those bonds were issued with net original issue premium of $18,629,212.85, which is itself counted against the total $555,000,000 authorization — so the first series consumed $189,999,212.85 of capacity, not $171,370,000, leaving roughly $365 million of the authorization for later series.

The Board now authorizes the second series in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $193,000,000 to pay the cost of the Projects and a portion of the associated issuance costs. Separately, Act 34 of the Public Acts of Michigan 2001 permits refunding of funded indebtedness, and the Board determines it is in the district's best interest to currently refund all or a portion of the 2016 School Building and Site Bonds dated December 28, 2016 — specifically those maturing May 1, 2027 through May 1, 2032 inclusive, the Refunded Bonds. Because the source of payment will be the same, and to reduce the cost of issuance and administration, the Board determines it makes practical and economic sense to combine the new money and refunding issues into a single series in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $220,000,000 while maintaining a separate capital projects fund for the Projects. A further recital preserves the option: if market interest rates rise so that refunding becomes noneconomic or inefficient, the Board intends to retain the ability to authorize only the $193,000,000 for the Projects.

The operative issuance provision restates the structure with a hard test. The portion issued for the Projects and associated issuance costs shall not exceed $193,000,000, and the balance of proceeds shall refund the Refunded Bonds. If the Authorized Officer, based on the advice of the Municipal Advisor, determines that the net present value savings associated with refinancing the Refunded Bonds is not at least 3.00% of the principal of the Refunded Bonds, the district may issue bonds not to exceed $193,000,000 for the Projects and issuance costs only — in which case the bonds are designated "2026 School Building and Site Bonds" and corresponding changes are made to the bond form, the name and purpose of the Debt Retirement Fund, and the application of proceeds.

Bond details: registered as to principal and interest in denominations of $5,000 or integral multiples, dated as of delivery or such other date as the Authorized Officer determines, maturing on May 1 and/or November 1 in years and amounts determined at sale, with final maturity not later than thirty years from the date of issue. Interest is at rates determined upon negotiated sale, not exceeding a true interest cost of 5.50% per annum, payable semi-annually on May 1 and November 1. The underwriter's discount shall not exceed 0.75% of principal. Principal is payable at a bank or trust company selected as Transfer Agent; interest by check mailed to the registered owner of record as of the fifteenth day of the month prior to each payment date. The bonds may be issued in book-entry-only form through The Depository Trust Company, and may be serial or term bonds subject to optional or mandatory redemption at times, in the manner and at prices determined at sale.

Four funds are established. The Debt Retirement Fund receives all proceeds from taxes levied for principal, interest and redemption price, unless a Common Debt Retirement Fund exists. The Capital Projects Fund receives the amounts specified at sale from net proceeds and any net original issue premium, used solely to pay Project costs and issuance costs, with any arbitrage rebate obligations to the U.S. Treasury under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. Costs of issuance go into a separate Cost of Issuance Fund, with remaining moneys allocated between the Capital Projects Fund and Debt Retirement Fund on bond counsel's advice; moneys remaining in the Capital Projects Fund after the Projects are complete may be used first for any purpose permitted by the 2022 Bond Proposal and second for any other purpose permitted by law. Any net original issue premium related to the new money portion is again counted against the 2022 Bond Proposal authorization. The Escrow Fund holds the balance of proceeds together with moneys transferred from the debt retirement funds for the Prior Bonds, held as cash or invested in direct or guaranteed obligations of the United States, in trust under an Escrow Agreement that irrevocably directs the trustee to call the specified Prior Bonds for redemption, with investments sufficient without reinvestment to pay principal and interest on the Refunded Bonds as they come due.

The unlimited tax covenant provides that commencing with the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2026 it is the duty of the district to levy a tax annually sufficient to pay principal and interest promptly when due, not subject to limitation as to rate or amount.

On method of sale, the district states it considered both competitive and negotiated sale and determined, per Act 34 and on the Municipal Advisor's advice, that a negotiated sale provides greater flexibility in structuring maturities and timing and will enable better marketing to the advantage of the district and its taxpayers. The Board appoints Huntington Securities, Inc. as senior managing underwriter, authorizes the Authorized Officer to appoint co-managing underwriters if recommended, and authorizes execution of the bond purchase agreement without further Board approval — subject to the stated parameters of 5.50% maximum true interest cost, at least 3.00% net present value savings measured against projected debt service on the Refunded Bonds absent the refunding under Treasury guidelines, and a maximum 0.75% underwriter's discount. The Authorized Officer is defined as the Superintendent and the Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, either acting individually.

Further provisions authorize application for bond ratings and municipal bond insurance if deemed appropriate; approval and execution of preliminary and final official statements with the standard 10b-5 representation that they contain no untrue statement of material fact and omit no material fact necessary to make the statements not misleading; and a continuing disclosure undertaking under SEC Rule 15c2-12. Tax matters covenants commit the district to maintaining the exclusion of interest from federal gross income. The reimbursement declarations under Treasury Regulation § 1.150-2 state that the maximum principal amount of debt expected to be issued for the Projects including issuance costs is $193,000,000, that reimbursement allocations will occur no later than 18 months after the later of payment or placed-in-service date and in no event more than three years after the original expenditure, and that the expenditures are capital expenditures under Treasury Regulation § 1.1.150-1(b).

The law firm of Miller, Canfield, Paddock and Stone, P.L.C. is appointed bond counsel, with the representation approved notwithstanding Miller Canfield's periodic representation in unrelated matters of the underwriter, Huntington Securities, Inc., and other potential parties — an express conflict waiver. PFM Financial Advisors LLC is appointed municipal advisor. The Authorized Officer is authorized to apply to the Michigan Department of Treasury for prior approval or to file a qualifying statement, to request rating waivers or exemptions, to have a Security Report prepared and filed under Act 34, and to submit a request for interim approval and other actions required for qualification under the School Bond Qualification, Approval, and Loan Act, Act 92 of the Public Acts of Michigan 2005.

Exhibit A sets out the bond form, naming Cede & Co. as registered owner and reciting the full faith and credit pledge, the 360-day year of twelve 30-day months, the authority under Act 451 of 1976 and Act 34 of 2001, and the certification that total indebtedness including this series does not exceed any constitutional or statutory limitation. Exhibit B is the form of continuing disclosure undertaking, requiring annual filing with the MSRB through EMMA on or before the last day of the sixth month after fiscal year end, commencing with the fiscal year ending June 30, 2026, of audited financial statements and operating data covering historical enrollment, state aid payments, property valuations, major taxpayers, tax rates per $1,000 of valuation, tax levies and collections, contributions to MPSERS, direct debt, the School Loan Revolving Fund program, and the current-year general fund budget summary — plus timely notice of the sixteen listed material events. Exhibit C is the form of application for final qualification of bonds.

Article I places the principal office at 2111 Pontiac Lake Road, Waterford Township, County of Oakland, and requires a continuously maintained registered office and registered agent.

Article III defines membership. Any publicly elected board of education member of a school district located in Oakland County, or any elected Oakland ISD board member, whose district is also a member in good standing of the Michigan Association of School Boards, is an eligible general member. Each member is entitled to one vote on each matter submitted to a vote, and all voting on business or elections before the members is done in person. The exception matters: each member school district has one vote on resolutions under Article IX and on bylaws amendments under Article XVI, recorded upon receipt of a completed resolution or ballot indicating the vote of that district's trustees, and must be received before the deadline on the ballot, with results provided to all member districts no later than the next general membership meeting. Electronic voting rights are granted to the Board of Directors only, to conduct emergency business, with all electronic votes reaffirmed at the next board meeting. Membership is not transferable or assignable.

Article IV provides that the Association is financed by an annual MASB grant to its County Area School Boards Association members, intermediate school district membership dues in an amount not to exceed the MASB CASBA grant, and contributions and gifts.

Article V governs member meetings. There shall be an annual meeting and not less than three additional regular membership meetings each year, the annual meeting being the first regular meeting after July 1. Special meetings may be called by voice or email by the President or by two or more directors with thirty days' notice. Written notice stating place, day and hour is delivered personally or by email not less than ten nor more than fifty days before the meeting. A quorum is the presence of at least one member from twenty-five percent of the member school districts. Superintendents and administrators of member districts are encouraged to participate. Section 3, on place of meeting, carries the first clerical redline: "the registered off office of the Association," with the rationale "Grammar and clarification. 'off' is supposed to be 'office'."

Article VI governs election of the Board of Directors. The Board consists of an odd number of directors, no fewer than seven and no more than nine, with discretion to set the number to best meet the Association's needs — a change to be considered whenever an election produces fewer candidates than open seats and before seeking candidates to fill a vacancy. Decreases are accomplished by attrition, which may produce an eight-member board for up to one year; increases by election, with the option of a mid-year special election. Any member is eligible, but only one member per district may serve at a time. Terms are three years. By May 1 each year the Board convenes an Election Committee comprising the three most recently elected directors, which seeks candidates creating geographical balance throughout Oakland County; application forms go to all member districts; nominations cannot be made from the floor at the election meeting; elections occur at the June meeting, by written ballot if there are more candidates than vacancies. Directors may resign by written notice or be removed with cause as defined in Appendix I by affirmative vote of a majority of the members or directors then in office, excluding the subject of the action. Failure to attend three consecutive board meetings constitutes a resignation, though the Board may grant an excused absence on written request to the President within thirty days.

Article VII governs the Board of Directors. Special meetings may be called by the President or any two directors. Section 4, on notice, carries a substantive redline: notice of any special meeting shall be given at least two days by written notice delivered personally, by phone, fax, or email — with the fax reference and the entire "or five days' notice by mail" alternative and its deemed-delivery sentence struck, on the rationale of "Deleting language that refers to sending meeting notices via US mail and fax which are outdated modes of communication." A majority constitutes a quorum. Directors receive no stated salaries but may be allowed a fixed sum and attendance expenses. Section 9 provides that the records and business of all Board of Directors proceedings shall be confidential and not subject to disclosure without the Board's advance authorization. Section 10 is added in full: the Board of Directors shall create and maintain Board Operating Procedures to be used in conjunction with these bylaws, on the rationale that the Board recently adopted such procedures further defining roles, responsibilities and timelines.

Article VIII covers officers — a President, Vice-President, Secretary and Treasurer elected from the current Board as soon as practical after the annual appointment of directors. Section 2 carries the "Ther The term of office" redline with its grammar rationale, and provides that any officer may be removed with cause by affirmative vote of a majority of directors. The President is Chief Executive Officer with general and active management, executing authorized conveyances and contracts and presiding at director meetings. The Vice-President acts in the President's absence. Section 6, the Secretary, adds that at the discretion of the Board of Directors on an annual basis the office may be divided into two roles, Corresponding Secretary and Recording Secretary, on the rationale that with a board of seven to nine directors splitting the role is helpful and provides additional leadership opportunities. The Treasurer has custody of funds and securities, keeps full and accurate accounts, deposits monies in designated depositories, disburses funds as ordered taking proper vouchers, and renders account to the President and directors; if required, the Treasurer gives a bond satisfactory to the directors. All officers may be required to furnish bonds, at the Association's cost.

Article IX governs committees. A quorum is twenty-five percent of appointed representatives, each present representative having one vote, with alternates counted only when the primary representative is absent. Section 3 carries the timing redline: each standing and ad hoc committee elects a chairperson annually from appointed representatives, as the first order of business at the committee's first meeting after January 31st — struck and replaced with July 1st — on the rationale that the operating year is July 1 to June 30 and the change brings the committees into alignment. Written notice of the election must be given at least seven calendar days ahead. Chairs establish and distribute meeting schedules and agendas, maintain attendance records, distribute minutes and report regularly to the Board through the President, and may be removed without cause by majority vote.

Section 4 makes the Government Relations Committee a standing committee whose purpose is to receive information on legislative matters for sharing with member districts, meeting at least six times per year; the redline adds "on" after "information" for grammar. Each member district should appoint a representative at its annual organizational meeting. A chairperson is elected annually at the first committee meeting after January 31st, each district in attendance casting one vote. A new sentence provides that in the absence of an elected Vice Chair, the Vice President of OCSBA assumes the position, on the rationale of building leadership on the committee. Legislative Priorities are reviewed and revised annually, submitted to the Board for approval, then provided to the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee and member districts.

Section 5 makes the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee a standing committee that develops and manages the resolutions and bylaws process and meets at least once per year. The redline changes appointment of committee members from "the Board of Directors" to "OCSBA President" annually, on the rationale that common practice is for the President to make committee appointments; members may be reappointed and elect a chairperson at the first meeting after appointment, and the Government Relations Committee Chairperson is a member. Resolutions or bylaws revisions may be initiated by a member district board, the Board of Directors, the Government Relations Committee or the Resolutions and Bylaws Committee, and once approved by the Board the Legislative Priorities are included in the resolutions drafted by the committee. The Board reviews all proposals before submission to member districts, which are asked to vote at their next meeting, with a voting window of at least forty calendar days. Resolutions approved by at least nineteen member school districts become the official position of the Association as interpreted and pursued by its Board of Directors — the provision cited at the head of every OCSBA resolutions circulation.

Article X provides for dissolution under Article VIII of the Articles of Incorporation and prohibits inurement of net earnings to any member, director or officer, as prohibited by Section 501(c)(4) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986 or the Michigan General Sales Tax Act or Use Tax Act.

Article XI sets fiduciary and financial responsibilities. Expenditures shall not exceed the approved annual budget, and no committee may create financial liability unless specifically authorized by a majority of the members. Board of Directors approval and signatory by both the President and Treasurer are required for any expenditure exceeding $2,500; expenditures up to $2,500 must be approved by either the President or the Treasurer; if either is absent or disabled the Vice-President may approve. The Treasurer completes reports on a timely basis and distributes them to all board members quarterly or on request; presents a budget for the upcoming fiscal year, July 1 to June 30, no later than the June board meeting; and presents end-of-year revenue and expense reports no later than August 30. The approved budget and annual report of income and expenditures are presented at the first fall member meeting, and accounting records are closed annually in preparation for IRS filings. Annually the Association performs certain agreed-upon procedures on its financial records, with the year-end report available to the Board before the annual board and member meetings; an external audit is conducted in place of the agreed-upon procedures only if required by law or a third party. The Board may enter an Administrative and Financial Services Agreement with Oakland Schools, with the Treasurer monitoring that work.

Article XII provides eleven sections of indemnification of officers, directors, employees and agents to the fullest extent authorized by the Michigan Nonprofit Association Act, covering third-party claims and claims brought by or in the right of the Association; barring indemnification for actions brought by the indemnitee unless authorized by the Board or brought to enforce the article successfully; setting the approval mechanism by disinterested directors, a committee of at least two disinterested directors, or independent legal counsel's written opinion; requiring prompt advancement of expenses on an unsecured undertaking to repay; permitting partial indemnification and indemnification of employees and agents; preserving other rights while capping total advancement at actual expenses incurred; authorizing liability insurance whether or not the Association would have power to indemnify; and providing severability and definitions extending "other enterprises" to employee benefit plans.

Article XIII leaves the fiscal year to the Board of Directors' determination — notable against Article XI's explicit July 1 to June 30 budget cycle.

Article XIV covers conflicts. Section 1 states the policy that all officers, directors, committee members and employees avoid conflicts between individual interests and those of the Association. Section 2 carries the duplicate-phrase redline, striking the repeated "or between the Association and one or more of its directors or officers," and provides that a contract or transaction involving an interested director is not void or voidable solely for that reason if it is fair and reasonable when authorized, or if the material facts are disclosed and the transaction is approved by sufficient vote without counting the interested director. Section 3 requires notice of any direct or indirect interest and abstention from voting or attempting to exert influence. Section 4 provides that a director with a conflict shall not be counted in determining the quorum for the meeting at which the matter is acted upon, even when permitted by law, and that the minutes shall reflect the disclosure, the abstention and the quorum situation.

Article XV covers miscellaneous provisions on contracts, execution of instruments, borrowing and adjourned meetings. Section 5 carries the electronic-notice redline: notice shall be given "by mailing electronic communication" to a director or officer at their last known district-provided email address, deemed given "at the time of such mailing communication," on the rationale that OCSBA does not physically mail communications. Section 6 permits action by unanimous written consent filed with the minutes. Section 7 permits remote participation by conference telephone or similar two-way communication equipment, which constitutes presence in person. Section 8 describes the corporate seal.

Article XVI covers amendments. Section 1 provides that bylaws may be altered or amended by vote of the member school districts, with the Board providing a written ballot and at least a forty-day voting period, one vote per district — and adds the new sentence that grammatical errors which do not change the meaning or intent of the language may be corrected by the Board of Directors without a vote of the membership, on the rationale that small grammar and spelling errors can be fixed during the annual review rather than going out to the membership. Section 2 permits additional rules and regulations that are not inconsistent with the Articles of Incorporation or bylaws unless a local, state or national emergency has been declared. Section 3 provides that in a declared local, state or national emergency the Board may set aside rules and regulations within the bylaws regarding the conduct of meetings and elections and the conduct of the Association's affairs.

Appendix 1 defines cause for removing a board member or officer, adopted by the OCSBA Board of Directors on September 16, 2020. Its preface sets out the three primary legal duties of a nonprofit board: the duty of care, ensuring prudent use of all assets including facility, people and good will; the duty of loyalty, ensuring activities and transactions advance the mission first, recognizing and disclosing conflicts of interest, and making decisions in the best interest of the nonprofit rather than of any individual board member or for-profit entity; and the duty of obedience, ensuring the nonprofit obeys applicable laws and regulations, follows its own bylaws, and adheres to its stated corporate purposes. It notes that board members also contribute to culture, strategic focus, effectiveness and financial sustainability and serve as ambassadors and advocates.

Cause is then defined as any of: acts of malfeasance, misfeasance or nonfeasance; willful failure to follow OCSBA bylaws; willful neglect of duties; failure to disclose a conflict of interest or using the Association for personal gain; using their position on the OCSBA Board of Directors or OCSBA's logo in a political endorsement, as such could reasonably be misconstrued as an endorsement by the Association; frequently missed board or committee meetings; creating an unhealthy or dysfunctional boardroom through inappropriate behavior or disrespecting other members; and ethical concerns such as discrimination, harassment or criminal behaviors. The appendix closes by noting that removal should only be done when absolutely necessary, but that the reasons for doing so are up to the Association's other directors and members.

Article XII provides eleven sections of indemnification of officers, directors, employees and agents to the fullest extent authorized by the Michigan Nonprofit Association Act, covering third-party claims and claims brought by or in the right of the Association; barring indemnification for actions brought by the indemnitee unless authorized by the Board or brought to enforce the article successfully; setting the approval mechanism by disinterested directors, a committee of at least two disinterested directors, or independent legal counsel's written opinion; requiring prompt advancement of expenses on an unsecured undertaking to repay; permitting partial indemnification and indemnification of employees and agents; preserving other rights while capping total advancement at actual expenses incurred; authorizing liability insurance whether or not the Association would have power to indemnify; and providing severability and definitions extending "other enterprises" to employee benefit plans.

Article XIII leaves the fiscal year to the Board of Directors' determination — notable against Article XI's explicit July 1 to June 30 budget cycle.

Article XIV covers conflicts. Section 1 states the policy that all officers, directors, committee members and employees avoid conflicts between individual interests and those of the Association. Section 2 carries the duplicate-phrase redline, striking the repeated "or between the Association and one or more of its directors or officers," and provides that a contract or transaction involving an interested director is not void or voidable solely for that reason if it is fair and reasonable when authorized, or if the material facts are disclosed and the transaction is approved by sufficient vote without counting the interested director. Section 3 requires notice of any direct or indirect interest and abstention from voting or attempting to exert influence. Section 4 provides that a director with a conflict shall not be counted in determining the quorum for the meeting at which the matter is acted upon, even when permitted by law, and that the minutes shall reflect the disclosure, the abstention and the quorum situation.

Article XV covers miscellaneous provisions on contracts, execution of instruments, borrowing and adjourned meetings. Section 5 carries the electronic-notice redline: notice shall be given "by mailing electronic communication" to a director or officer at their last known district-provided email address, deemed given "at the time of such mailing communication," on the rationale that OCSBA does not physically mail communications. Section 6 permits action by unanimous written consent filed with the minutes. Section 7 permits remote participation by conference telephone or similar two-way communication equipment, which constitutes presence in person. Section 8 describes the corporate seal.

Article XVI covers amendments. Section 1 provides that bylaws may be altered or amended by vote of the member school districts, with the Board providing a written ballot and at least a forty-day voting period, one vote per district — and adds the new sentence that grammatical errors which do not change the meaning or intent of the language may be corrected by the Board of Directors without a vote of the membership, on the rationale that small grammar and spelling errors can be fixed during the annual review rather than going out to the membership. Section 2 permits additional rules and regulations that are not inconsistent with the Articles of Incorporation or bylaws unless a local, state or national emergency has been declared. Section 3 provides that in a declared local, state or national emergency the Board may set aside rules and regulations within the bylaws regarding the conduct of meetings and elections and the conduct of the Association's affairs.

Appendix 1 defines cause for removing a board member or officer, adopted by the OCSBA Board of Directors on September 16, 2020. Its preface sets out the three primary legal duties of a nonprofit board: the duty of care, ensuring prudent use of all assets including facility, people and good will; the duty of loyalty, ensuring activities and transactions advance the mission first, recognizing and disclosing conflicts of interest, and making decisions in the best interest of the nonprofit rather than of any individual board member or for-profit entity; and the duty of obedience, ensuring the nonprofit obeys applicable laws and regulations, follows its own bylaws, and adheres to its stated corporate purposes. It notes that board members also contribute to culture, strategic focus, effectiveness and financial sustainability and serve as ambassadors and advocates.

Cause is then defined as any of: acts of malfeasance, misfeasance or nonfeasance; willful failure to follow OCSBA bylaws; willful neglect of duties; failure to disclose a conflict of interest or using the Association for personal gain; using their position on the OCSBA Board of Directors or OCSBA's logo in a political endorsement, as such could reasonably be misconstrued as an endorsement by the Association; frequently missed board or committee meetings; creating an unhealthy or dysfunctional boardroom through inappropriate behavior or disrespecting other members; and ethical concerns such as discrimination, harassment or criminal behaviors. The appendix closes by noting that removal should only be done when absolutely necessary, but that the reasons for doing so are up to the Association's other directors and members.
